content: Overmedication occurs when a healthcare provider prescribes medications that are either unnecessary or excessive for a patient. This can happen for several reasons, such as the prescriber being unaware of other medications the patient is already taking, a lack of knowledge about potential drug interactions with other chemicals or within specific populations, or due to human error. In some cases, overmedication is intentional and may even be illegal, such as the use of excessive psychoactive medications as chemical restraints for elderly patients in nursing homes. The potential side effects of overmedication include slowed reaction times, which can affect speech, movement, and thought processes. Patients may also experience sleeplessness, increased confusion, an unsteady gait, constipation, dry mouth, blurry vision, heightened agitation, and involuntary repetitive movements of the tongue, feet, hands, or trunk. In severe cases, hallucinations may occur. Overmedication can also result from patients taking more medication than prescribed or indicated on over-the-counter (OTC) product labels. This may happen either intentionally or unintentionally. Additionally, patients may unknowingly take both prescription and nonprescription drugs that contain the same active ingredients, leading to excessive dosing. For example, a patient taking a prescription medication like Vicodin, which contains both hydrocodone and acetaminophen, might also take an OTC product like Tylenol, which contains acetaminophen as its active ingredient. This overlap can result in overmedication. Similarly, overmedication can occur when patients are prescribed or take additional drugs—whether prescription or OTC—that produce the same or similar therapeutic effects. For instance, if a patient is taking a prescription-strength ibuprofen product and also uses a naproxen product (either prescription or OTC), this combination can constitute overmedication. Such practices can be dangerous, potentially harmful to the patient’s health, and may increase overall healthcare costs. Patients may also overmedicate themselves by taking their medications at shorter intervals than prescribed or recommended on the container label. This behavior can lead to the accumulation of medications in the body at higher levels than intended, resulting in unwanted side effects. In some cases, these side effects can be severe, even life-threatening.
